steps.message:
You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

The work is almost certainly recoverable - either in a stash, on a side branch, or as a dangling commit that the reflog will reveal. I need to look at all of these before doing anything that could overwrite them.
Plan: Run a set of read-only inspection commands: git status, branch list, stash list, a full reflog, and the reflog for the current HEAD. That should show exactly where the missing changes went. Once I see the result I can pick the right way to bring them back.

steps.message:
Analysis: The reflog has it all. The user's two commits ('off the job market woo' and 'Move to Stanford') exist at c499730, which was the tip of an old master. They then checked out HEAD~1 and reset the master branch back to that same earlier point, orphaning the two newer commits. Checking out master again simply left them stranded at that old commit. There is no stash to consult, and the commits were never on any other named branch, so that dangling reflog entry is the only place they still exist.
Plan: Create a temporary branch to point at c499730, confirm it holds the expected changes, and then merge it into master. After that I will clean up the now redundant temporary branch. A fast forward merge is expected since master has not advanced beyond the common ancestor.
steps.reasoning_content: Now the situation is clear. The user made two commits on the old master, then checked out HEAD~1, then reset master back to that same commit, and then checked out the new master. They lost two commits that way. I need to merge that branch back into master and bring it up to date. Let me first look at what those commits actually changed so I can confirm they're the ones I'm looking for.

The refused branch deletion is only a safety net against losing the work before the merge is finished. Getting to the bottom of the situation calls for looking at the exact lines in question.
Plan: Print the conflicting region of about.md along with some of the surrounding text so the two competing versions can be seen. That will show whether one side entirely supersedes the other or whether pieces of each need to be kept in the result.

I need to look at the conflicting section in that file, work out which wording to keep, or possibly preserve both. Since I'm unfamiliar with the user's intent, I'll examine the conflict markers directly. The rescue branch has to stay around until the conflict is resolved and committed, so it can't be deleted yet.

steps.message:
Analysis: The two versions are much closer than the markers make it seem. Each one lists the same prior positions, and the only real difference lies in the first sentence. The old side still describes the person as a sixth year PhD candidate at the University of Washington. The new side replaces that with a description of a postdoctoral position at Stanford, and the whole point of the lost commits was to put that newer information in. Once the older statement is discarded there is nothing further to choose between.
Plan: Rewrite the file to keep the Stanford sentence and the common list of previous positions while dropping the superseded line and all three marker lines. After the edit the usual check for leftover markers ought to find nothing. That in turn will let the interrupted merge be concluded by making the final commit for which git has already prepared a message.
steps.reasoning_content:
Now I can see the whole picture. Both versions keep the same list of previous positions, so none of that part needs to be picked one way or the other. The only point of disagreement is the first line. That line on the old side says the person is a sixth year PhD candidate at the University of Washington. The new side says they are a Postdoctoral Researcher at Stanford, and that is plainly what the two missing commits were meant to record. That first sentence is therefore the one to discard.

It would be a simple enough matter to just leave the Stanford line in place and to get rid of all the bookkeeping the merge left behind. The old sentence is now entirely superseded. I would rather to construct the result by taking everything that lies after the opening marker and then everything after the middle marker. That would automatically drop the old text as well as the three marker lines. It would be easy enough to do in a few editing passes. After that a check for remaining markers should come up empty.

One thing to keep in mind is that the old line is indented with a single space before the word previously. The new line has no such indentation. Since the new version is now the one that prevails it should be fine to let that line stand without the odd leading space. It would only add a bit more to clean up were that left in place.

steps.message:
Analysis: Everything went well right up to the final commit. With no editor installed on this machine, git could not open the prepared message for confirmation, so the merge is still hanging in the middle. The resolution itself is already staged and the log proves that nothing has been recorded yet. Git has also gone and left that message in the repository root, so there is no need to put together a substitute for it.
Plan: Use the file git has already prepared to record the pending commit, and then the old branch will count as entirely incorporated. That ought to allow the ordinary deletion of the branch to get through. A final look at the log will show that the missing work has been taken over by master.
steps.reasoning_content: The commit didn't actually happen because the editor is missing. The resolved file is staged, but the merge is still in a suspended state. I can confirm this from the fact that the log still has the old tip at the very top. There is a prepared merge message that can be applied from the file that git has left in the root of the repository, and that would be preferable to devising something new. Once that has been done, the rescue branch will have been completely incorporated and will therefore be safe to delete.
